Hi, thank you. Well, um, the main reason I’m here... it's just getting to be too much at work. I'm a registered nurse, and I work on a really busy floor. And I know nursing is always chaotic, I mean, I went through a rigorous graduate program for this, I should be able to handle a bustling environment, but I just... I lose my train of thought constantly. Like, absolutely constantly. 

It’s actually getting incredibly frustrating and honestly a bit scary because I’ll be right in the middle of figuring out a really complicated patient flow issue—you know, trying to figure out who is discharging, who needs to be moved to step-down, coordinating all the moving parts—and then, just, the slightest thing happens. An IV pump starts beeping three rooms down, or I hear someone asking another nurse a totally unrelated question down the hall, or a call light goes off, and it's like... poof. My brain just completely resets. 

Suddenly I’m standing there at the nurses' station and I’ve completely forgotten what patient flow issue I was even working on. I just stare at my computer screen trying to remember what I was doing ten seconds ago. And I have to start all over again, looking at my report sheet, trying to retrace my mental steps. It doesn't just happen once in a while, it happens all shift long, every single shift, and I just can't keep functioning like this. It takes so much energy just to try and force my brain to stay on track when literally any noise pulls me away.

Oh, absolutely. It’s... honestly, it’s everywhere. It’s not just at the hospital, though that’s where the stakes feel the highest. But at home? My personal life is just a complete disaster right now. I forget things that should be completely routine, basic adulting things, you know? 

Like, my mom or my sister will call me, and I’ll be in the middle of making dinner or folding scrubs, so I think, 'Okay, I'll call them right back as soon as I finish this one thing.' And I genuinely mean to! I have every intention of doing it, I really do. But then three days go by, and they're texting me asking if I’m alive or if I'm mad at them, and I feel terrible because the thought literally never crossed my mind again. 

Or, um, bills. Paying a bill at home should be so simple, right? You get the bill, you pay it. But I’ll set the mail on the kitchen counter, and it just ceases to exist in my brain. Even if I set an alarm on my phone! I’ll literally set a reminder that says 'pay electric bill,' the alarm goes off, I swipe it away because I’m, I don't know, tying my shoes or walking out the door, and I completely forget again. I have late fees on things I easily have the money to pay for, just because I can't remember to click a button.

Well, um... anxious or depressed? I mean, I guess it depends on how you define it. Like, I wouldn't say I'm waking up every day feeling this deep, dark sadness, you know? I don't feel hopeless about life in general. I love my dog, I love my family, I actually really love nursing when I can actually function properly. But... I do get incredibly down on myself. I feel this constant, low-level panic that I'm dropping balls left and right, and I just don't know which one is going to shatter when it hits the ground. It's exhausting. I'll be trying to fall asleep, and my heart will just be racing because I'm trying to mentally audit my entire day to make sure I didn't miss a critical lab value or forget to call a doctor back. So, yes, I feel very anxious, but it's not like... a generalized anxiety about the world. It's a very specific, intense anxiety about my own brain and how unreliable it is. It's like I can't trust myself, and that is a terrifying way to live. I just feel so wound up all the time trying to compensate for the fact that my attention span is basically zero.

Physical symptoms? Um, well, no, not really. I mean, I know I just said my heart races when I'm trying to fall asleep, but it's not like... it's not like actual palpitations, if that makes sense? Oh, sitting still? No, not really. I mean, I wasn't the kid bouncing off the walls or disrupting the class, which is probably why nobody ever flagged anything as being wrong back then. I was a pretty quiet kid. But paying attention... wow, yes. It has always been a massive struggle. And honestly, reading them was like looking in a mirror. 

Every single teacher, year after year, wrote basically the exact same comments. Even in elementary school, my teachers wrote that I was bright, which was nice, I guess, but then they would immediately follow it up by saying I was careless. That specific word came up so much. Careless. And it hurt, because it wasn't that I didn't care! I really did. But I was just always, always losing my worksheets. I would somehow lose a piece of paper between the teacher handing it to me and me getting back to my desk. Or I would actually do the work—I would sit there and finish all the math problems—and then the next day I would completely forget to turn my homework in. It would just sit crumpled at the absolute bottom of my backpack for weeks until a teacher sent a note home. 

It got to the point where my mom had to intervene so heavily. She had to sit with me at the kitchen table every single night just to keep me on track. She couldn't just tell me to go do my homework in my room like my sister did, she had to physically sit right next to me. If she got up for even a second to check on dinner or answer the phone, I would just drift off and start staring at the wall or doodling in the margins of my notebook. She had to micromanage my entire evening, checking my folders, making sure the papers were actually in the bag so I could hand them in the next morning. So yeah, the physical hyperactivity wasn't really my issue, but my brain... my attention has just been wandering off like that for as long as I can remember.

Well, I mean, like I was just saying with the report cards and my mom having to help me, the... the baseline struggle has definitely always been there. Act on impulse? Blurting things out? Um, no. Honestly, no, not at all. If anything, I have the exact opposite problem. I overthink everything to death before I actually do or say anything, probably because I'm so terrified of making a mistake.

It's like my brain is moving a hundred miles an hour, but it's just spinning its wheels in the mud. I'm never acting quickly on those thoughts. So the blurting out or acting without thinking... that's really not me at all. I think way too much, if that makes sense. Just... usually not about the right things at the right time.

Diagnosed? No. No, never. Which honestly, when I really sit down and think about it now, is just... it's incredibly frustrating. Because it feels like I've been struggling so loudly my entire life, but because I wasn't, you know, causing a scene or being disruptive, I just completely slipped through the cracks. I just spent my whole life thinking I was fundamentally flawed, or broken, or just not trying hard enough. If she got up for even a second to check on dinner or answer the phone, I would just drift off and start staring at the wall or doodling in the margins of my notebook. She had to micromanage my entire evening, checking my folders, making sure the papers were actually in the bag so I could hand them in the next morning. Extreme anger? Um... no. No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I definitely get emotional, but it’s not... it’s not anger or irritability, really. It’s more just this crushing sense of being completely overwhelmed. Like, I don’t lash out at people. If anything, I just internalize all of it. 

Like, I remember this one shift last week, it was just a nightmare. The medication dispenser was down, so we couldn't get any of our scheduled meds out, and a patient's family member was at the desk just screaming at me about a food tray being late, which, you know, I have absolutely zero control over the kitchen. And in that moment, I wasn't angry at the family member, and I wasn't irritable with my nurses who were all looking at me to fix the machine. I just felt this intense, heavy panic in my chest, like I was failing everyone. So I excused myself, went into the clean utility room, shut the door, and just cried for like two minutes. Oh, absolutely. Yes. All the time. It's actually becoming a huge problem for me at work right now, especially since I took on this charge nurse role. Because now, on top of everything else, I have these administrative duties, right? And one of the big ones is this focused chart review. I have to do these audits of the documentation across different shifts—checking to make sure all the care plans are updated, verifying that the fall risk assessments were charted correctly by the previous nurses, that kind of thing. 

And if I know a task is going to take that kind of deep, focused attention... I just... I keep pushing it off. I will literally do anything else. Sitting down with it feels like trying to climb a massive brick wall. Just the thought of having to open up those files and force my brain to process all that dense, tedious information line by line makes my chest feel incredibly tight. It's this overwhelming sense of dread, like my brain is just screaming at me that it's too hard and I can't do it. 

So instead of just sitting down and getting it over with, I'll find all these little bedside tasks to do instead. I'll go restock the isolation carts, which isn't even my job anymore, or I'll go hunt down a bladder scanner for one of the newer nurses. I'll volunteer to help someone turn a heavy patient or go hang a new bag of IV fluids. I just keep bustling around the unit, doing all these physical, immediate things. And the funny thing is, to everyone else on the floor, I probably look like this incredibly helpful, proactive team player. They probably think, wow, she's so hands-on and supportive! 

But the reality is, I am just running away. I'm running away from the computer because the anxiety of having to sit still and sustain that mental effort is just too much. I'll tell myself, okay, I'll start the audit right after I check on room 12. And then after room 12, I'll say, well, let me just go empty the sharps containers first, just to be safe. And suddenly it's the end of my twelve-hour shift, the audit still isn't done, and the next charge nurse is coming in, and I have to either stay an hour late to force myself to do it when I'm already exhausted, or I have to pass it off and make some excuse. Which just makes me feel incredibly guilty and incompetent. But I just can't make myself start it. It really does feel like hitting a physical wall. She had to micromanage my entire evening, checking my folders, making sure the papers were actually in the bag so I could hand them in the next morning. So yeah, the physical hyperactivity wasn't really my issue, but my brain... my attention has just been wandering off like that for as long as I can remember.\n\nDoctor: Have you always had trouble with focus and memory, or did it start to become a significant problem at some point in your life?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean, like I was just saying with the report cards and my mom having to help me, the... the baseline struggle has definitely always been there. I've always had to work twice as hard just to keep my head above water, you know? Through college, nursing school, my first few years on the floor... I survived by basically living and dying by my planner and a million sticky notes. So the trouble with focus was always lingering in the background. But as far as it becoming a truly significant problem? Like, to the point where I feel like I'm completely drowning and actually failing at life? That is more recent. This has really been a major problem since I took on the expanded charge-nurse responsibilities almost two years ago. \n\nI mean, at the time, I was so flattered they offered it to me. It felt like this huge validation of my clinical skills, so of course I said yes. But I had no idea how much it would completely break my brain. Because before, when I was just a regular floor nurse, I had my specific patients for a twelve-hour shift. I could make my little checklist, put my head down, and just power through my own tasks. But as charge nurse... oh my gosh, it is a totally different world. You aren't just managing your own tasks, you are the central hub for the entire unit. The phone is constantly ringing, doctors are grabbing you in the hallway, families are complaining at the desk, and you're trying to figure out bed assignments while three different nurses are asking you for help. It is just a relentless, non-stop barrage of interruptions. \n\nAnd that's where my memory just absolutely shatters. Someone will ask me to pull a med override, and on the way to the machine, the unit secretary tells me a critical lab value came in, and by the time I write the lab value down, I have completely, one hundred percent forgotten about the nurse waiting for the medication. It just evaporates from my mind. I thought it was just a learning curve at first, you know? I kept telling myself, 'Oh, you just need to get used to the new workflow, you'll figure it out.' But it's been almost two years of this now, and it's not getting better. If anything, it's getting worse because I'm just so burnt out from trying to overcompensate. The sheer volume of things I'm supposed to keep track of now in this role is just... it's completely exposed whatever deficits I've been hiding all these years.\n\nDoctor: Do you often act on impulse or blurting out answers without thinking?\n\nPatient: Act on impulse? I overthink everything to death before I actually do or say anything, probably because I'm so terrified of making a mistake. \n\nLike, if we're doing interdisciplinary rounds on the unit—which is already incredibly stressful—and the attending physician looks right at me and asks a direct question, like what the patient's overnight urine output was or if they tolerated their morning meds... even if I literally just looked at the chart five minutes ago, I won't just blurt out the answer. I completely freeze. I second-guess myself instantly. I'll think, 'Wait, was it 400 cc's or 500? Did I mix up room 12's output with room 14's?' I make them wait while I verify it. \n\nAnd in regular conversations, like with my husband or my friends, I'm definitely not the one interrupting or talking over people. Usually, I'm the one who's awkwardly quiet because I've completely zoned out while they were talking. My mind is usually a million miles away, thinking about a patient I handed off three days ago or a grocery list I lost, and then suddenly I'll realize the person is looking at me, waiting for a response, and I have absolutely no idea what they just said. I have to do that embarrassing thing where I ask them to repeat the last five minutes of the conversation. \n\nSo, no, I'm definitely not impulsive with my words. I don't really do things on impulse either. I'm too busy agonizing over every little detail, trying to make sure I haven't forgotten something critical. Oh, my gosh, yes. It is... it’s honestly a disaster. And it’s so embarrassing because, as a nurse, you’re supposed to be this absolute master of time management, right? Like, that’s literally day one of clinicals, they drill it into you. But I just... I can’t do it. I really can't.

Restless? Oh, gosh, no. Honestly, it's the exact opposite for me. I mean, maybe some people get like that, bouncing their leg or needing to pace around or whatever, but I just... I really don't have the physical energy for it. 

Like I was saying earlier about the hospital, working those twelve-hour shifts on your feet, running from room to room, dealing with the patients and the doctors and trying to keep track of the charting... by the time I actually get a moment where I don't strictly need to be active, my body is just completely, utterly done. When I sit down on the couch at home, I am practically glued to the cushions. My husband will ask if I want to go for a walk or just do something around the house, and I just look at him like he has two heads because I physically cannot fathom moving my legs anymore. 

So, no, I don't get fidgety at all. If anything, I'm just incredibly lethargic when I'm not actively being forced to move by my job. I'll just sit there, staring at the wall or scrolling on my phone, not even really processing what I'm looking at, just totally paralyzed by how exhausted I am. I actually kind of wish I had a little bit of that restless energy sometimes, you know? Like, maybe if I was a little restless, I'd actually get up and fold that laundry I was talking about, or I'd walk over and finally pay that water bill sitting on the island. But no, my body just completely shuts down. 

It's more of an internal thing, I guess? Like my brain is bouncing all over the place, spiraling about the appointments I missed or the charge nurse duties I messed up, but physically? No. I am completely still. Just... a total lump. So, yeah, I definitely wouldn't say I feel restless or need to fidget. I'm usually just desperately trying to rest.

I forget to do it. It’s like if it’s not actively on fire right in front of my face, it just falls out of my head, no matter how many sticky notes or phone reminders I try to use. It makes me feel so incredibly unreliable and flaky, and I hate it, because I really, really try to be on top of these things.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling anxious or depressed lately?\n\nPatient: Well, um... anxious or depressed? When I realize I've missed another appointment, or when I'm standing at the nurses' station for the fifth time in an hour trying to remember what I was doing, I just feel this overwhelming sense of failure. I beat myself up about it constantly. I'll go home after a shift and just replay all the moments where my brain glitched, and I think, 'Why are you like this? I feel this constant, low-level panic that I'm dropping balls left and right, and I just don't know which one is going to shatter when it hits the ground. It's exhausting. I'll be trying to fall asleep, and my heart will just be racing because I'm trying to mentally audit my entire day to make sure I didn't miss a critical lab value or forget to call a doctor back. It’s not that we don’t have the money to pay it, I just completely forget the bill exists until my husband asks why we got a late fee. \n\nAnd appointments are a total nightmare. I missed my dentist appointment just a few weeks ago, and the absolute worst part about it is that I actually put it in my phone calendar! I did the thing you're supposed to do! I set a reminder for the day before, and I set another reminder for two hours before. And somehow, when that two-hour reminder went off on my phone, I just glanced at it, swiped it away because I was in the middle of sorting a pile of mail, and I told myself, \"Okay, I'll go get my shoes on in five minutes.\" And then three hours later I was still sitting on the floor with the mail and realized I had completely missed the entire appointment. I felt so incredibly stupid having to call the receptionist and apologize yet again. \n\nIt just happens with everything. Like, I forget things even when I have every intention of doing them.
